items.title: British women got the vote in two instalments: 1918 and 1928
items.claim: When did UK women win equal voting rights with men?

options.text: 1918 — full equal franchise immediately after WWI
1918 gave the vote to women over 30 meeting property qualifications (around 8.4 million); 1928 (Equal Franchise Act) gave it to all women over 21 on the same terms as men

items.reveal:
The Representation of the People Act 1918 enfranchised women over 30 who were householders, married to householders, occupiers of property at £5+ rent or university graduates. Men got the vote at 21 (or 19 if a serviceman).

The WSPU (Pankhursts, 1903), the NUWSS (Millicent Fawcett, constitutionalist) and women's war work all contributed. The 1918 compromise was partly designed to keep women a minority of the electorate.

The Equal Franchise Act 1928 gave women the vote at 21 on the same terms as men. Emmeline Pankhurst died on 14 June 1928, weeks before it took effect.
items.why: Reform is rarely complete in one step. The 10-year gap between 1918 and 1928 is itself part of the history — a partial victory deliberately designed to limit female political weight.

items.title: Edwin Chadwick's 1842 report drove the 1848 Public Health Act
items.claim: What was the immediate origin of British public health legislation?

options.text: A spontaneous parliamentary initiative without prior research

Edwin Chadwick's 'Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population' (1842) documented appalling urban conditions; the cholera epidemic of 1848-49 (around 53,000 dead in England and Wales) prompted the Public Health Act 1848 creating the General Board of Health and local boards
Disraeli's 1875 Act was the first such law
The 1848 Act applied only to Scotland

items.reveal:
Chadwick was a Poor Law commissioner and disciple of Jeremy Bentham. His report, partly self-funded, argued that disease and poverty were linked to environmental conditions — drains, water, ventilation, cesspits.

The 1848 Public Health Act was permissive: local boards could be established by petition or where mortality exceeded 23 per 1,000. The 1875 Public Health Act under Disraeli made provisions compulsory and gave local authorities effective powers over water, sewers, housing, food and nuisance.

John Simon (chief medical officer from 1855) institutionalised the role of medical officers of health across the country.
items.why: Modern state public health did not begin with the NHS. It began with sanitarian engineers and statisticians in the 1840s-70s, who treated mortality data as a political argument.

items.title: The English Reformation was not popular
items.claim: What did Eamon Duffy's 'The Stripping of the Altars' (1992) argue?

options.text: That the English laity were already Protestant in spirit before 1530 and welcomed the changes
That late medieval Catholicism was vigorous and popular, and the Reformation was imposed from above against widespread reluctance
That the Reformation made no real impact below the level of the elite
That the Pilgrimage of Grace (1536) succeeded in halting reform

items.reveal:
Duffy used churchwardens' accounts, wills and surviving objects to argue that late medieval English Catholic devotion was rich, complex and widely engaged — not a corrupt system waiting to be reformed.

The Pilgrimage of Grace (1536) involved perhaps 40,000 northern rebels protesting against the dissolution. The 1549 Western Rising opposed the new Prayer Book. Mary I's restoration of Catholicism (1553-1558) was popular in much of the country.

A. G. Dickens's older 'English Reformation' (1964) had emphasised popular Protestant momentum; Duffy reversed that picture.
items.why: Whether a change was 'demanded from below' or 'imposed from above' is a structural question about how change works. Both can be true at once, but the balance matters for how we read the period.
